title: Introduction
text:
Running CONTENTO
CONTENTO can be executed in three different ways depending on your computational environment and familiarity with containerized software. We strongly recommend the Docker-based workflows, as they guarantee complete reproducibility across operating systems and avoid dependency conflicts.

Option 1: Run using Docker (recommended)
If Docker is not yet installed on your system, we recommend you install Docker Desktop from the official website, since it provides a friendly graphic interface to manage your images and keep your Docker Engine up-to-date. If you already have Docker installed, running CONTENTO requires a single command from your terminal (make sure your Docker Desktop is running):

docker run \
    --rm \
    -p 3838:3838 \
    -v $(pwd)/inst:/srv/shiny-server/app/inst \
    ghcr.io/klemonlab/contento:latest

The terminal window will show the app startup and soon will start accepting connections. When you see the message that the app is listening, open your web browser (any browser) and navigate to:
http://localhost:3838
This approach provides a fully reproducible computational environment with all R, Bioconductor, and system dependencies pre-installed.

Rebuilding image from scratch
A Dockerfile is included in the repository so that users familiar with building container images can self-build with docker build -t contento . if necessary.



Option 2: Run using Docker Compose
For users who prefer a persistent local setup and the convenience of a preconfigured container mount, CONTENTO can also be launched using Docker Compose. To do this, make sure you have the compose plugin installed (it is bundled with modern distributions of Docker Desktop by default) by running

docker compose --help

The helper string for the compose plugin should come up.
Then, clone the CONTENTO repository:

git clone https://github.com/klemonlab/contento.git

To start the application, navigate to the working directory and simply run:

cd contento
docker compose up

Or run it in the background:

docker compose up -d

Once the container starts, access the application again at:
http://localhost:3838


Option 3: Run locally within R/RStudio
Some users may prefer to execute CONTENTO directly from an existing R installation, usually used in conjunction with the popular IDE RStudio.
Clone the CONTENTO repository:

git clone https://github.com/klemonlab/contento.git

After opening the project (CONTENTO.Rproj) within Rstudio, install the dependencies by running:

install.packages(c(
    "shiny",
    "shinydashboard",
    "shinycssloaders",
    "DT",
    "plotly",
    "tidyverse",
    "purrr",
    "viridis",
    "RColorBrewer",
    "ComplexUpset",
    "scales",
    "ggiraph",
    "gridExtra",
    "patchwork"
))

if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager"))
    install.packages("BiocManager")

BiocManager::install(c(
    "ComplexHeatmap",
    "DESeq2",
    "fgsea",
    "msigdbr",
    "circlize",
    "SummarizedExperiment"
))

Open app.R in RStudio and click the interactive :arrow_forward: Run App button, or execute:

shiny::runApp("app.R")

The application will then become available in your web browser.



Which option should I choose?

title: Create Genome Annotations for CONTENTO
text:
Annotation files are optional in CONTENTO, but they enable many of the platform’s most useful features. Depending on your organism and the identifiers used in your SummarizedExperiment (SE) object, functionality may be limited without an annotation file. In particular, annotation files are used for:

Functional enrichment analysis (GSEA/GESECA)
Displaying informative gene labels and symbols
Genomic neighborhood analysis (bacterial genomes only)



CONTENTO can perform functional enrichment analysis using gene sets from two sources:

Annotation-Based Gene Sets: Available for any organism through a user-provided annotation data frame (.rds format). Required elements:

A Geneid column matching the rownames() of the SE object.
One or more functional annotation columns containing gene set assignments (e.g. COG categories, KEGG pathways, GO terms, regulons, custom categories). Multiple values per gene should be separated by !!! (e.g., "GO:0006415!!!GO:0016149"). CONTENTO will parse them by counting the gene as belonging to each category for functional enrichment analysis.

MSigDB Gene Sets: Available only for human, mouse, and other species supported by msigdbr R package. It requires:

metadata(se)$organism must exactly match a valid msigdbr species name (e.g. Homo sapiens, Mus musculus, etc.).
Gene identifiers must be Ensembl gene IDs (ENSG..., ENSMUSG..., etc.), either: directly in rownames(se), or in a column of the annotation file containing Ensembl IDs. CONTENTO automatically detects Ensembl identifier columns when present.





Annotation files also improve the general CONTENTO experience.

Gene symbols/labels can be displayed throughout tables and visualizations instead of raw gene identifiers. This is especially useful for bacteria, where Geneid is often a locus tag (e.g. SAUSA300_0001) and not not an informative label like the associated gene name or product description.
Genomic neighborhood analysis, which additionally requires start, end, strand columns in the annotation file. This is a beta feature available only when metadata(se)$organism is exactly “Bacteria”)

title: Create Genome Annotations for CONTENTO
section: 1.1 Ensembl-Based Organisms (Human, Mouse, other msigdbr Species)
text:
1.1 Ensembl-Based Organisms (Human, Mouse, other msigdbr Species)
For organisms distributed through Ensembl, download the same GTF and genome assembly used during RNA-seq analysis. The genome FASTA is not required to create a CONTENTO annotation file, but is often downloaded alongside the GTF because both are used during alignment, genome indexing, or other downstream analyses.
Example: Human GRCh38 (Ensembl Release 113)

FILES_DIR="inst/extdata/genomes" 
GENOME_NAME="Homo_sapiens.GRCh38" 
VERSION=113

# Gene annotation file used here and in the downstream analysis
wget -P "$FILES_DIR" \
  "https://ftp.ensembl.org/pub/release-${VERSION}/gtf/homo_sapiens/${GENOME_NAME}.${VERSION}.gtf.gz"

# Reference genome used in the downstream analysis (alignment/quantification)
wget -P "$FILES_DIR" \ 
  "https://ftp.ensembl.org/pub/release-${VERSION}/fasta/homo_sapiens/dna/${GENOME_NAME}.dna_sm.primary_assembly.fa.gz"

title: Create Genome Annotations for CONTENTO
section: 1.2 NCBI/RefSeq-Based Organisms (Bacteria and Other Non-Ensembl Genomes)
text:
1.2 NCBI/RefSeq-Based Organisms (Bacteria and Other Non-Ensembl Genomes)
For organisms that are not maintained in Ensembl, the preferred annotation source is typically the NCBI RefSeq assembly. These annotations are distributed as GFF3 and GenBank (.gbff) files and contain gene coordinates, locus tags, product descriptions, and other metadata that can be incorporated into CONTENTO annotation files.

Option A: Download from the NCBI Assembly Website

Go to NCBI Assembly
Search for your genome accession (e.g., GCF_000013465.1 for Staphylococcus aureus subsp. aureus FPR3757)
Download the assembly in GFF3 format
Unzip and save in your working directory



Option B: Download Using the NCBI Datasets CLI
For reproducible workflows, the NCBI Datasets command-line tool is recommended.

# Install NCBI Datasets CLI if you haven't already. This should be run in your terminal.
conda activate ncbi_datasets 

# Update the genome accession and directory as needed
FILES_DIR="inst/extdata/genomes" 
GENOME_NAME="GCF_000013465.1" 

# Update to download the desired files (genome sequence, GenBank flat file, GFF3...)
datasets download genome accession "$GENOME_NAME" \
            --include genome,gbff,gff3,seq-report \
            --filename "$FILES_DIR/$GENOME_NAME.zip"
            
# Unzip
unzip "$FILES_DIR/$GENOME_NAME.zip" -d "$FILES_DIR"
# Individual files can be renamed to include the genome name for easier identification.

The accompanying GenBank file (.gbff) is optional for CONTENTO itself but is useful for downstream tools such as anvi’o, Prokka, or Bakta.

title: Create Genome Annotations for CONTENTO
text:
1.3 Generate your own GFF3 file (Optional)
For newly assembled genomes or organisms lacking public annotations, you may generate your own annotation files using tools such as Prokka or Bakta. These tools typically produce GFF3 files that can be processed using the same workflow described below. Regardless of the annotation source, the resulting GFF3 should contain stable gene identifiers (e.g. locus_tag) that correspond to the identifiers used in downstream RNA-Seq quantification.

title: Create Genome Annotations for CONTENTO
text:
2.1 From a GTF (Ensembl)
We can import Geneid from the gene_id attribute in the GTF file using rtracklayer, along with other useful information such as gene name and biotype.

# Set up your R environment and read the GTF file. Adapt based on the GTF name and location
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(rtracklayer)

GENOMES_DIR <- here("inst/extdata/genomes")
GENOME_NAME <- "Homo_sapiens.GRCh38.113"

# Import GTF file
gtf_data <- import(file.path(GENOMES_DIR, paste0(GENOME_NAME, ".gtf.gz")))

# Extract gene annotations. For available column names check colnames(mcols(gtf_data))
annotations <- data.frame(
  Geneid = mcols(gtf_data)$gene_id,
  gene = mcols(gtf_data)$gene_name,
  biotype = mcols(gtf_data)$gene_biotype
)
# Sanity check: Ensure there are no duplicated Gene IDs
annotations <- annotations[!duplicated(annotations$Geneid), ]

# Save the annotations to a CSV/RDS file
write_csv(annotations, file.path(GENOMES_DIR, paste0(GENOME_NAME, "_annot.csv")))
saveRDS(annotations, file.path(GENOMES_DIR, paste0(GENOME_NAME, "_annot.rds")))

title: Create Genome Annotations for CONTENTO
Create Genome Annotations for CONTENTO
text:
3.1 Merge Custom Annotations
You can merge annotations from any source that contains gene identifiers (Gene IDs). These can be sourced from:

Public repositories
Your own experimental data (e.g., Tn-seq, RNA-seq, proteomics)
Manually curated annotations from literature searches

In this example, we demonstrate using RegPrecise regulon annotations, but the same approach works for any custom annotation file.






Found a Useful Annotation Source?



Open an issue on GitHub to share it with the community! Include the name, URL, and how you used it.



Requirements and Format
Key requirement: Your custom annotation file must have a column with gene identifiers that match the Geneid column in your GTF/GFF3 derived annotations. This column might have a different name in your custom file (e.g., “Geneid”, “Gene ID”, “Locus tag”, …), but it should contain the same values as Geneid.
Important notes:

Columns: Your custom annotation file can have as many additional columns as you want. All columns will be merged into the final dataframe, or you can select only a subset of columns before merging. In the merging step, you can add a prefix to custom annotation columns (e.g., RegPrecise_, reg_) to avoid name clashes and easily identify annotation sources.
Gene coverage: No requirement for the same number of genes as in the GTF/GFF3 derived annotations, as long as there is a common key (Geneid) for merging. Genes in GTF/GFF3 derived annotations without a corresponding custom annotation entry will be included in the final dataframe with NA values for the custom columns.
Multiple annotations per gene: There should be only one entry per gene in the custom annotation file. If a gene has multiple annotations, concatenate them into a single string separated by !!! (e.g., "regulon1!!!regulon2"). See the anvi’o example below for how to concatenate multiple values. CONTENTO will parse these and count the gene as belonging to each category for functional enrichment analysis.


# Set up your R environment and read the anvi'o annotation file. Adapt based on the file name and location
library(tidyverse)
library(here)

GENOMES_DIR <- here("inst/extdata/genomes")
GENOME_NAME <- "GCF_000013465.1"

# Load your GFF3-derived annotations
annotations <- read_csv(file.path(GENOMES_DIR, paste0(GENOME_NAME, "_annot.csv")))

# Load custom annotation file tab delimited
custom_annot <- read_delim(file.path(GENOMES_DIR, "USA300_FPR3757_RegPrecise.txt"))

# Merge the custom annotations with the GFF3-derived annotations using locus_tag as the key
annotations_merged <- annotations |>
  left_join(custom_annot, by = c("Geneid" = "locus_tag")) |> # Adjust to the "Geneid" column name in your custom annotation file
  rename_with(
    ~ paste0("RegPrecise_", .), # Prefix custom annotation columns to avoid name clashes with GFF3-derived annotations
    -all_of(colnames(annotations))  
  ) 

# Save the annotations to a CSV/RDS file
output_file <- file.path(GENOMES_DIR, paste0(GENOME_NAME, "_annot_RegPrecise.csv"))
write_csv(annotations_merged, output_file)
saveRDS(annotations_merged, file.path(GENOMES_DIR, paste0(GENOME_NAME, "_annot_RegPrecise.rds")))

title: Create Genome Annotations for CONTENTO
text:
3.2 Enhance Annotations with Anvi’o (Bacterial Genomes)
Anvi’o is a comprehensive platform that integrates multiple annotation sources and can be used to generate a rich annotation file for bacterial genomes. It can be run on any genome in GenBank format and will produce a single annotation file with multiple functional annotations for each gene.

HMMs - Generic protein domain detection
COG24 - Clusters of Orthologous Groups (excellent for functional enrichment)
KEGG - Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes pathways (excellent for functional enrichment)
Pfams - Protein family annotations
CAZymes - Carbohydrate-active enzyme classification


Run Anvi’o Annotation Pipeline
For more details on how to run anvi’o see the Anvi’o documentation.

# Install Anvio if you haven't already. This should be run in your terminal.
conda activate anvio-9

# Update the genome accession and directory as needed
FILES_DIR="inst/extdata/genomes" 
GENOME_NAME="GCF_000013465.1" 

# Process the GenBank file to extract gene calls, functions, and fasta sequences 
anvi-script-process-genbank -i "$FILES_DIR/$GENOME_NAME.gbff" \
--output-gene-calls "$FILES_DIR/${GENOME_NAME}_calls.txt" \
--output-functions "$FILES_DIR/${GENOME_NAME}_prodigal.txt" \
--output-fasta "$FILES_DIR/${GENOME_NAME}.fa" \
--annotation-source prodigal \
--include-locus-tags-as-functions

# Create anvi'o contigs database from the fasta file and gene calls
anvi-gen-contigs-database -f "$FILES_DIR/${GENOME_NAME}.fa" \
-o "$FILES_DIR/${GENOME_NAME}_anvio.db" \
--external-gene-calls "$FILES_DIR/${GENOME_NAME}_calls.txt" \
-n "$GENOME_NAME"

# Import functions from prodigal output
anvi-import-functions -c "$FILES_DIR/${GENOME_NAME}_anvio.db" \
-i "$FILES_DIR/${GENOME_NAME}_prodigal.txt"

# Run HMM annotations 
anvi-run-hmms -T 8 -c "$FILES_DIR/${GENOME_NAME}_anvio.db"

# Run NCBI COG annotations with DIAMOND
anvi-run-ncbi-cogs -T 8 --search-with diamond -c "$FILES_DIR/${GENOME_NAME}_anvio.db"

# Run KEGG KOfam annotations
anvi-run-kegg-kofams -T 8 -E 1e-15 -c "$FILES_DIR/${GENOME_NAME}_anvio.db"

# Run Pfam domain annotations
anvi-run-pfams -T 8 -c "$FILES_DIR/${GENOME_NAME}_anvio.db"

# Run CAZyme annotations
anvi-run-cazymes -T 8 -c "$FILES_DIR/${GENOME_NAME}_anvio.db"

# Export all functions to text file
anvi-export-functions -c "$FILES_DIR/${GENOME_NAME}_anvio.db" \
-o "$FILES_DIR/${GENOME_NAME}_annot.txt"

# Export contigs stats and database info
anvi-display-contigs-stats "$FILES_DIR/${GENOME_NAME}_anvio.db" \
--report-as-text -o "$FILES_DIR/${GENOME_NAME}_stats.txt"

anvi-db-info "$FILES_DIR/${GENOME_NAME}_anvio.db" &>> "$FILES_DIR/${GENOME_NAME}_log.txt"



Parse Anvi’o Annotations into CSV
The resulting anvi’o annotation file contains comprehensive functional annotations for each gene, which can be parsed into a CSV format with the following R code.

# Set up your R environment and read the anvi'o annotation file. Adapt based on the file name and location
library(tidyverse)
library(here)

GENOMES_DIR <- here("inst/extdata/genomes")
GENOME_NAME <- "GCF_000013465.1"

# Read the anvi'o annotation 
anvio_annot <- read_delim(file.path(GENOMES_DIR, paste0(GENOME_NAME, "_annot.txt")), delim = "\t") |>
  mutate(source = as.factor(source)) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.character), trimws)) |>
  select(-e_value) |> # Exclude e-values to keep dataframe simple
  rename("acc" = "accession", "func" = "function") |> # Shorter names
  mutate(across(c(acc, func), trimws))

# Convert from long format (multiple rows per gene) to wide format (one row per gene)
anvio_annot <- anvio_annot |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = source,
    values_from = c(acc, func),
    values_fn = list(
      acc = ~ paste(unique(.), collapse = "!!!"), 
      func = ~ paste(unique(.), collapse = "!!!"))
  ) 



Parse KEGG Hierarchical Annotations
The KEGG annotations from anvi’o come as hierarchical levels separated by semicolons (e.g., “Metabolism; Carbohydrate metabolism; Glycolysis / Gluconeogenesis”). To facilitate functional enrichment analysis and gene exploration in CONTENTO, it’s useful to split these into separate columns for each level of the KEGG hierarchy (e.g., KEGG Group, KEGG Pathway).

# Split multiple KEGG annotations into separate rows (one row per KEGG annotation) 
anvio_annot <- anvio_annot |>
  separate_rows(func_KEGG_Class, sep = ",")

# Split into hierarchy levels (separated by ;)
anvio_annot <- anvio_annot |>
  separate(func_KEGG_Class, 
           into = c("func_KEGG_Class", "func_KEGG_Subclass", "func_KEGG_Pathway"),
           sep = ";",
           extra = "drop",
           fill = "right")

# Collapse back to one row per gene
anvio_annot <- anvio_annot |>
  group_by(across(-starts_with("func_KEGG_"))) |>
  summarise(
    func_KEGG_Class = paste(unique(na.omit(func_KEGG_Class)), collapse = "!!!"),
    func_KEGG_Subclass = paste(unique(na.omit(func_KEGG_Subclass)), collapse = "!!!"),
    func_KEGG_Pathway = paste(unique(na.omit(func_KEGG_Pathway)), collapse = "!!!"),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(across(starts_with("func_KEGG_"), ~ na_if(., "")))



Add AA Sequences to Annotations (Optional)
You can also merge the anvi’o annotations with the aa sequences from the calls file to have a comprehensive annotation dataframe with all the information for each gene. This can be useful for gene exploration in CONTENTO, where you can display the sequence along with the functional annotations for each gene.

# Read calls file to get aa sequences
anvio_calls <- read_delim(file.path(GENOMES_DIR, paste0(GENOME_NAME, "_calls.txt")), delim = "\t") |>
  select(gene_callers_id, aa_sequence)

# Merge with anvio_annot by gene_callers_id
anvio_annot <- anvio_annot |>
  left_join(anvio_calls, by = "gene_callers_id")



Merge Anvi’o Annotations
Finally, you should merge the anvi’o annotations with the GFF3-derived annotations and the custom annotations from RegPrecise to create a comprehensive annotation CSV file for CONTENTO.

# Load GFF3-derived annotations (with RegPrecise already merged, or use original if skipping section 3.1)
annotations <- read_csv(file.path(GENOMES_DIR, paste0(GENOME_NAME, "_annot_RegPrecise.csv")))

# Merge anvi'o annotations using GENBANK_LOCUS_TAG (the column added by anvi'o) as a key for merging, which should match the Geneid column in the GFF3-derived annotations. 
annotations_merged <- annotations |>
  left_join(anvio_annot, by = c("Geneid" = "func_GENBANK_LOCUS_TAG")) |> 
  rename_with(
    ~ paste0("anvio_", .), # Prefix anvio annotation columns 
    -all_of(colnames(annotations))  
  ) 

# Save the annotations to a CSV/RDS file
output_file <- file.path(GENOMES_DIR, paste0(GENOME_NAME, "_annot_RegPrecise_Anvio.csv"))
write_csv(annotations_merged, output_file)
saveRDS(annotations_merged, file.path(GENOMES_DIR, paste0(GENOME_NAME, "_annot_RegPrecise_Anvio.rds")))

title: Create SE for CONTENTO
text:
CONTENTO expects a single SummarizedExperiment (SE) object (.rds) containing expression data, differential expression results for every contrast, and descriptive metadata. This document walks through building that object using RSEM/tximport counts and DESeq2, but CONTENTO itself is agnostic to how the downstream analysis was performed. If you have a different quantification method (e.g. Salmon, STAR + featureCounts) or a different DE tool (e.g. edgeR, limma-voom), you can still build a compatible SE as long as you reproduce the following structure.
A CONTENTO-compatible SE has four required components:

assays: must contain an assay named expr_matrix, which provides the expression values used by CONTENTO visualizations and downstream analyses.
rowData: one row per gene, with DE statistics for each contrast stored as columns named <name>__<contrast_name> (double underscore separator, e.g. log2FC__VirusTvsF, padj__VirusTvsF). CONTENTO is agnostic to the DE tool used, but requires these exact generic statistic names: log2FC, stat and padj (required for every contrast), and log2FC_shrunk (optional). If your tool uses different names (e.g. DESeq2’s log2FoldChange, edgeR’s logFC), rename the columns to this vocabulary before building the SE (see Step 4 below). Any other columns you include (e.g. baseMean, lfcSE) are carried through but not used by CONTENTO.
colData: sample-level metadata (experimental factors used for grouping/coloring in plots).
metadata(se): a list with, at minimum, contrasts (a character vector of unique contrast names matching the __<contrast_name> suffixes described above). Optional fields organism and annotation unlock MSigDB-based GSEA and annotation loading, respectively (see the annotation article for details). Two further optional fields fine-tune the CONTENTO experience:

db_species: character string, "HS" or "MM". By default, CONTENTO picks the MSigDB source database automatically: "MM" (mouse-curated) only when organism is exactly "Mus musculus", and "HS" (human-curated) for every other msigdbr-supported organism. Set db_species to override that default — e.g. to force human-curated gene sets for a mouse dataset, or mouse-curated gene sets ortholog-mapped onto another species, instead of the automatic choice. Note that organism must still be a species msigdbr recognizes for ortholog mapping; db_species does not extend MSigDB support to organisms msigdbr doesn’t already support.
dataset_name: character string used as the base filename prefix for every file downloaded from CONTENTO (tables, plots, etc.). If omitted, CONTENTO falls back to the uploaded SE filename, or "CONTENTO" if that isn’t available either.









Feature
Required SE component




DE tables & volcano plots
rowData contrast columns


Expression Plot / Heatmap / GESECA
expr_matrix assay


Variance Decomposition tab
optional varpart_* rowData columns


MSigDB GSEA
metadata(se)$organism matching a valid msigdbr species (metadata(se)$db_species optionally overrides which source database — human or mouse — is queried)


Neighborhood Analysis (bacteria)
metadata(se)$organism == "Bacteria" + annotation with coordinates





Both examples below follow the same sequence:

Metadata Preparation: load sample metadata and set factor levels/labels.
Data Import: pull RSEM quantifications into a tximport object.
Exploratory DESeq2 Analysis (Optional): fit a simple model and inspect a PCA to inspect the data before committing to a final design.
Differential Expression Analysis: fit the full design, extract one or more contrasts, and rename output columns to CONTENTO’s generic vocabulary (log2FC, stat, padj).
Create Expression Matrix: extract the expression matrix for use in CONTENTO (normalization recommended).
Create SummarizedExperiment (SE) Object: assemble assays, rowData, colData, and metadata with convert_to_SE().

Example 1 covers a single two-group comparison (one contrast). Example 2 covers a multi-factor design with an interaction term, producing several related contrasts and also includes variance partitioning results.

# Set up your R environment
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(tximport)
library(DESeq2)
library(vsn)
library(edgeR)
library(variancePartition)
library(ashr)
library(SummarizedExperiment)

SE_DIR <- here("../inst/extdata/SE")

title: Create SE for CONTENTO
text:
Both examples below follow the same sequence:

Metadata Preparation: load sample metadata and set factor levels/labels.
Data Import: pull RSEM quantifications into a tximport object.
Exploratory DESeq2 Analysis (Optional): fit a simple model and inspect a PCA to inspect the data before committing to a final design.
Differential Expression Analysis: fit the full design, extract one or more contrasts, and rename output columns to CONTENTO’s generic vocabulary (log2FC, stat, padj).
Create Expression Matrix: extract the expression matrix for use in CONTENTO (normalization recommended).
Create SummarizedExperiment (SE) Object: assemble assays, rowData, colData, and metadata with convert_to_SE().

Example 1 covers a single two-group comparison (one contrast). Example 2 covers a multi-factor design with an interaction term, producing several related contrasts and also includes variance partitioning results.

# Set up your R environment
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(tximport)
library(DESeq2)
library(vsn)
library(edgeR)
library(variancePartition)
library(ashr)
library(SummarizedExperiment)

SE_DIR <- here("../inst/extdata/SE")

title: Create SE for CONTENTO
text:
Step 1. Metadata Preparation
meta must contain one row per sample, a file_base column matching your RSEM output filenames, and the experimental factor columns used in the design formula below.

# Read metadata file
project_name <- "ExpSingleContrast"
meta <- read_csv(file.path(SE_DIR, paste0(project_name, "_metadata.csv")))

# Create unique condition and label for each sample. This will be used by CONTENTO for visualization.
meta <- meta |>
  mutate(
    virus = factor(virus, levels = c("FALSE", "TRUE")),
    exp = factor(exp),
    label = interaction(virus, exp, sep = " | ") # unique label for each sample 
  )

title: Create SE for CONTENTO
text:
Step 2. Data Import
The tximport [@tximport] function reads in gene-level quantification results from RSEM and organizes them into a structured list for downstream analysis. It extracts estimated counts, transcript lengths, and abundance values, ensuring compatibility with DESeq2 and other Bioconductor workflows. Since some transcripts may have a reported length of 0, we update those to 1 to prevent issues ensuring valid calculations during analysis.

# Import data using tximport
rsem_folder <- file.path(SE_DIR, "rsem_counts")
count_files <- file.path(rsem_folder, paste0(meta$file_base, ".genes.results"))
names(count_files) <- meta$label
txi <- tximport(count_files, type = "rsem", txIn = FALSE, txOut = FALSE)
txi$length[txi$length == 0] <- 1

title: Create SE for CONTENTO
text:
Step 3. Exploratory DESeq2 Analysis
We run an initial DESeq model design to explore the data. This exploratory fit is only used for the PCA check below — it is not the design used for contrast extraction, which comes next.

# DESeq design 
dds <- DESeqDataSetFromTximport(txi,
                                colData = meta,
                                design = ~ virus + exp)

# Run DESeq
dds <- DESeq(dds)


Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
PCA calculated based on the VST normalized [@tibshirani1988; @huber2003; @Anders2010] data using ntop=500 top features by variance. Samples from different experiments were interspersed rather than clustered, suggesting that the experimental batch effect was not a major source of variation in the data.

vsd <- vst(dds, blind = TRUE)
pcaData <- plotPCA(vsd, intgroup = c("virus", "exp"), returnData = TRUE)
percentVar <- round(100 * attr(pcaData, "percentVar"))
Bac.Vir_colors = c("#CC9564", "#856141")
Bac.Vir_fill <- c("white", "#856141")

ggplot(pcaData, aes(PC1, PC2)) +
  geom_point(aes(fill = virus, color = virus, 
                 shape = exp), 
             size = 4, stroke = 1) +  
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(23, 25, 21)) + 
  scale_color_manual(values = Bac.Vir_colors) + 
  scale_fill_manual(values = Bac.Vir_fill) +
  ggtitle("Principal Component Analysis (blind = TRUE)") +
  xlab(paste0("PC1: ", percentVar[1], "% variance")) +
  ylab(paste0("PC2: ", percentVar[2], "% variance")) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  ) +
    guides(
    color = guide_legend(title = "virus", override.aes = list(color = Bac.Vir_colors, shape = 22))
  )

title: Create SE for CONTENTO
Create SE for CONTENTO
text:
Step 5. Create Expression Matrix
The expression matrix stored in the SE can be generated using any normalization or transformation method appropriate for your dataset. CONTENTO treats this assay as a matrix of expression values used for visualization and downstream analyses such as expression plots, heatmaps, and GESECA. Common choices include VST-transformed counts from DESeq2, log-CPM values from edgeR, or log-transformed TPM values.
For RNA-seq workflows based on DESeq2, we recommend using the variance stabilizing transformation (VST), which reduces the dependence of variance on expression level while preserving biological signal. This generally produces expression values that are well suited for visualization and exploratory analyses in CONTENTO.

expr_matrix <- assay(vst(dds, blind = FALSE))

title: Create SE for CONTENTO
text:
Step 6. Create SummarizedExperiment (SE) Object
The convert_to_SE() helper below builds the final SE object. It reshapes the long-format differential expression results into the wide-format rowData structure expected by CONTENTO, where each statistic is stored in a separate column with the pattern <statistic>__<contrast_name>. It attaches sample metadata as colData, stores the expression matrix in the expr_matrix assay, optionally merges variance-partition results as varpart_* columns, and records contrasts, organism, annotation, db_species, and dataset_name in metadata(se). The same function can be reused regardless of experimental design or the number of contrasts being included.

convert_to_SE <- function(dds, contrasts_df, expr_matrix,
                          organism = NULL, annotation = NULL, varpart = NULL,
                          db_species = NULL, dataset_name = NULL) { 
  
  # Reshape to wide format
  contrasts_wide <- contrasts_df %>%
    pivot_wider(
      id_cols = Geneid,
      names_from = contrast,
      values_from = -c(Geneid, contrast),
      names_sep = "__"
    )
  
  contrasts_found <- unique(contrasts_df$contrast)
  cat("✓ Found", length(contrasts_found), "contrasts:", paste(contrasts_found, collapse = ", "), "\n")
  
  # Extract sample metadata
  sample_metadata <- as.data.frame(colData(dds))
  
  # Create rowData with Geneid as rownames
  rowdata_df <- contrasts_wide %>%
    column_to_rownames("Geneid")
  
  # Add variance partition data if provided
  if (!is.null(varpart)) {
    cat("Loading variance partition data...\n")
    
    tryCatch({
      # Extract only the variance partition matrix
      varpart_matrix <- varpart$varPart
      
      # Get common genes between rowData and varPart
      common_genes <- intersect(rownames(rowdata_df), rownames(varpart_matrix))
      
      if (length(common_genes) > 0) {
        # Convert to dataframe and add varpart_ prefix
        varpart_df <- as.data.frame(varpart_matrix[common_genes, , drop = FALSE])
        colnames(varpart_df) <- paste0("varpart_", colnames(varpart_df))
        
        # Merge with rowdata_df (only for genes that exist in both)
        rowdata_df[common_genes, colnames(varpart_df)] <- varpart_df
        
        cat("✓ Added variance partition for", length(common_genes), "genes\n")
        cat("  Factors:", paste(gsub("varpart_", "", colnames(varpart_df)), collapse = ", "), "\n")
      } else {
        cat("⚠ No common genes between contrasts and variance partition\n")
      }
      
    }, error = function(e) {
      cat("⚠ Error loading variance partition:", e$message, "\n")
    })
  }
  
  # Ensure rowData order matches dds
  rowdata_df <- rowdata_df[rownames(dds), ]
  
  # Verify dimensions match
  stopifnot(identical(rownames(rowdata_df), rownames(dds)))
  stopifnot(identical(rownames(sample_metadata), colnames(dds)))
  
  cat("✓ Gene order verified:", nrow(rowdata_df), "genes match\n")
  
  # Create SummarizedExperiment
  se <- SummarizedExperiment(
    assays = list(expr_matrix = expr_matrix),
    colData = DataFrame(sample_metadata),
    rowData = DataFrame(rowdata_df)
  )
  
  # Store metadata
  metadata(se) <- list(
    design = design(dds),
    contrasts = contrasts_found,
    organism = organism,
    annotation = annotation, 
    db_species = db_species,      # optional: "HS" or "MM", overrides automatic msigdbr routing
    dataset_name = dataset_name,  # optional: base filename prefix for CONTENTO downloads
    date = Sys.Date()             # recorded for reproducibility but not read by CONTENTO itself
  )
  
  # Return the SummarizedExperiment object

  cat("  Dimensions:", nrow(se), "genes x", ncol(se), "samples\n")
  cat("  Assays:", paste(names(assays(se)), collapse = ", "), "\n")
  cat("  Columns in rowData:", ncol(rowData(se)), "\n\n")
  
  return(se)
}


SE = convert_to_SE(
  dds = dds,
  contrasts_df = contrasts_df,
  expr_matrix = expr_matrix,
  organism = "Homo sapiens", 
  annotation = "Homo_sapiens.GRCh38.113_annot",
  dataset_name = "ExpSingleContrast"
  # db_species is left NULL here because "Homo sapiens" already defaults to "HS";
  # set e.g. db_species = "MM" to instead query mouse-curated gene sets
  # ortholog-mapped onto this organism, overriding the automatic "HS" default.
)

✓ Found 1 contrasts: VirusTvsF 
✓ Gene order verified: 78932 genes match
  Dimensions: 78932 genes x 6 samples
  Assays: expr_matrix 
  Columns in rowData: 7 

saveRDS(SE, file.path(SE_DIR, paste0(project_name, "_SE.rds")))

title: Create SE for CONTENTO
text:
Step 1. Metadata Preparation
meta must contain one row per sample, a file_base column matching your RSEM output filenames, and the experimental factor columns used in the design formula below.

# Read metadata file
project_name <- "ExpMultContrast"
meta <- read_csv(file.path(SE_DIR, paste0(project_name, "_metadata.csv")))

# Create unique condition and label for each sample. This will be used by CONTENTO for visualization.
meta <- meta |>
  mutate(
    bacteria = factor(bacteria, levels = c("NB", "Spn", "Hin", "Dpi")), # NB (No-Bacteria) is the reference level
    virus = factor(virus, levels = c("FALSE", "TRUE")),
    exp = factor(exp),
    condition = interaction(bacteria, virus, sep = "_"), # unique condition for each sample
    label = interaction(bacteria, virus, exp, sep = " | ") # unique label for each sample 
  )

title: Create SE for CONTENTO
text:
Step 2. Data Import
Same import procedure as Example 1, applied to this project’s samples.

# Import data using tximport
rsem_folder <- file.path(SE_DIR, "rsem_counts")
count_files <- file.path(rsem_folder, paste0(meta$file_base, ".genes.results"))
names(count_files) <- meta$label
txi <- tximport(count_files, type = "rsem", txIn = FALSE, txOut = FALSE)
txi$length[txi$length == 0] <- 1

title: Create SE for CONTENTO
text:
Step 3. Exploratory DESeq2 Analysis
We run an initial DESeq model design to explore the data. It does not consider the interaction between variables. We only use it to explore the data and possible effects for the 3 independent experiments. The design formula is ~ bacteria + virus + exp, which accounts for the main effects of bacteria, virus, and experiment without considering their interactions. This allows us to assess the individual contributions of each factor to gene expression changes. This exploratory fit is only used for the PCA check below, it is not the design used for contrast extraction, which comes later.

# DESeq design 
dds <- DESeqDataSetFromTximport(txi,
                                colData = meta,
                                design = ~ virus + bacteria + exp)

# Run DESeq
dds <- DESeq(dds)


Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
PCA calculated based on the VST normalized [@tibshirani1988; @huber2003; @Anders2010] data using ntop=500 top features by variance. Samples from different experiments were interspersed rather than clustered, suggesting that the experimental batch effect was not a major source of variation in the data.

vsd <- vst(dds, blind = TRUE)
pcaData <- plotPCA(vsd, intgroup = c("bacteria", "virus", "exp"), returnData = TRUE)
percentVar <- round(100 * attr(pcaData, "percentVar"))
Bac.Vir_colors = c("#CC9564", "#a89de0", "#f54590", "#2e67f2", "#856141","#6855c9","#9f2d5e", "#1e439d")
Bac.Vir_fill <- c("white", "white", "white", "white", "#856141","#6855c9","#9f2d5e", "#1e439d")

ggplot(pcaData, aes(PC1, PC2)) +
  geom_point(aes(fill = condition, color = condition, 
                 shape = exp), 
             size = 4, stroke = 1) +  
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(23, 25, 21)) + 
  scale_color_manual(values = Bac.Vir_colors) + 
  scale_fill_manual(values = Bac.Vir_fill) +
  ggtitle("Principal Component Analysis (blind = TRUE)") +
  xlab(paste0("PC1: ", percentVar[1], "% variance")) +
  ylab(paste0("PC2: ", percentVar[2], "% variance")) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  ) +
    guides(
    color = guide_legend(title = "condition", override.aes = list(color = Bac.Vir_colors, shape = 22))
  )










Variance Partitioning Analysis
In this more complex design we are also interested in quantifying the contribution of each factor (virus, bacteria, and experiment) to the overall variance in gene expression. This is particularly important for understanding how much of the observed variability can be attributed to biological factors versus technical or experimental factors. CONTENTO allows users to visualize the variance partitioning results for each gene, providing insights into the relative importance of each factor in shaping gene expression patterns.
Gene-level expression values were modeled using precision weights estimated with the limma::voom() transformation, which accounts for the mean–variance relationship in RNA-seq data. Lowly expressed genes can be filtered using edgeR::filterByExpr(), which removes genes with insufficient counts for reliable statistical analysis and improves the stability of downstream variance estimates.
We use the variancePartition [@hoffman2017] package, which quantifies the proportion of variance in gene expression attributable to each factor in a linear mixed model.

run_varPart_analysis <- function(txi, meta, formula_vp, formula_fixed, filter_low_expr = TRUE) {
  # Align meta to sample order
  meta <- as.data.frame(meta)
  meta <- meta[match(colnames(txi$counts), meta$label), ]
  rownames(meta) <- meta$label
  stopifnot(identical(rownames(meta), colnames(txi$counts)))

  # Design matrix: only fixed effects (for voom & filterByExpr)
  design <- model.matrix(formula_fixed, data = meta)

  # Normalize counts
  counts <- DGEList(txi$counts)
  counts <- normLibSizes(counts)

  # Filter low-expressed genes
  if (filter_low_expr) {
    keep <- filterByExpr(counts, design)
    counts_used <- counts[keep, ]
  } else {
    counts_used <- counts
  }

  # logCPM values with voom
  v <- voom(counts_used, design)

  # Fit variance partition model (supports random effects)
  varPart <- fitExtractVarPartModel(v, formula_vp, meta)

  # Format results
  varPart_df <- as.data.frame(varPart)
  varPart_df$Geneid <- rownames(varPart_df)

  # Return
  return(list(v = v, varPart = varPart, varPart_df = varPart_df))
}

Use formula_fixed with fixed effects (required for the design matrix step) while formula_vp is used to decompose variance across bacteria/virus/exp as random intercepts

formula_fixed <- ~ virus + bacteria + exp          # for voom/filterByExpr design matrix
formula_vp <- ~ (1|virus) + (1|bacteria) + (1|exp)   # for variance partitioning you can't mix fixed and random categorical variables in the same call 

varPart <- run_varPart_analysis(txi, meta, formula_vp, formula_fixed, filter_low_expr = T)
plotVarPart(varPart$varPart)

title: Create SE for CONTENTO
text:
Step 4. Differential Expression Analysis
This design captures all the variables of interest. - virus + bacteria + virus:bacteria Includes main effects of virus and bacteria, as well as their interaction. This allows us to test whether the effect of virus depends on the species. This is equivalent to virus * bacteria. - exp To account for the batch effect of the 3 independent experiments, we include the experiment as a covariate in the model. This helps to control for any variability introduced by differences between experiments.

# DESeq design 
dds <- DESeqDataSetFromTximport(txi,
                                colData = meta,
                                design = ~ virus + bacteria + virus:bacteria + exp)

# Run DESeq
dds <- DESeq(dds)


Generate Contrast Results

Virus TRUE vs FALSE in each Species
This section tests the effect of virus infection (TRUE vs FALSE) within each bacterial species specifically:

For the reference bacteria condition (NB), the virus effect is captured by the main coefficient virus_TRUE_vs_FALSE.
For other bacteria conditions (Spn, Hin, Dpi), the virus effect is a combination of the main virus effect plus the interaction term (e.g., virusTRUE.bacteriaDpi).


contrast_list_Virus_TvsF <- list(
  VirusTvsF_NB  = "virus_TRUE_vs_FALSE",                                   
  VirusTvsF_Spn = list(c("virus_TRUE_vs_FALSE", "virusTRUE.bacteriaSpn")), 
  VirusTvsF_Hin = list(c("virus_TRUE_vs_FALSE", "virusTRUE.bacteriaHin")), 
  VirusTvsF_Dpi = list(c("virus_TRUE_vs_FALSE", "virusTRUE.bacteriaDpi"))  
)
results_Virus_TvsF <- imap(contrast_list_Virus_TvsF, function(contrast_val, name) {
  if (is.character(contrast_val)) {
    run_contrast_analysis(dds, contrast_name = name, coef = contrast_val)
  } else {
    run_contrast_analysis(dds, contrast_name = name, contrast = contrast_val)
  }
})



Difference in Virus Effect Compared to NB
Here we focus on whether the virus effect differs between each bacteria condition and relative to the reference NB. This highlights species-specific modulation of virus response by comparing the virus effect in each bacteria against the baseline virus effect in NB.

We use the interaction terms alone (e.g., virusTRUE.bacteriaDpi), which quantify how much the virus effect in each species deviates from that in NB.


contrast_list_VirusInteract_vsNB <- list(
  VirusInteract_Dpi = "virusTRUE.bacteriaDpi",
  VirusInteract_Spn = "virusTRUE.bacteriaSpn",
  VirusInteract_Hin = "virusTRUE.bacteriaHin"
)
results_VirusInteract_vsNB <- imap(contrast_list_VirusInteract_vsNB, ~ run_contrast_analysis(dds, contrast_name = .y, coef = .x,))



Bacteria vs NB in Virus FALSE
This comparison evaluates how each bacterial species differs from the reference NB when virus is absent (virus = FALSE). This reveals baseline species-specific gene expression differences without virus influence.

Because virus FALSE is the baseline in the model, these contrasts use only the main bacteria effects (e.g., bacteria_Dpi_vs_NB).


contrast_list_Bacteria_vsNB_VF <- list(
  DpivsNB_VF = "bacteria_Dpi_vs_NB",
  SpnvsNB_VF = "bacteria_Spn_vs_NB",
  HinvsNB_VF = "bacteria_Hin_vs_NB"
)
results_Species_vsNB_VF <- imap(contrast_list_Bacteria_vsNB_VF, ~ run_contrast_analysis(dds, contrast_name = .y, coef = .x))



Bacteria vs NB in Virus TRUE
Here we test the bacteria differences under virus infection (virus = TRUE). This reveals species-specific gene expression differences that might occur under virus influence.

These contrasts combine the main bacteria effect plus the interaction with virus (e.g., bacteria_Dpi_vs_NB + virusTRUE.bacteriaDpi).


contrast_list_Bacteria_vsNB_VT <- list(
  DpivsNB_VT = list(c("bacteria_Dpi_vs_NB", "virusTRUE.bacteriaDpi")),
  SpnvsNB_VT = list(c("bacteria_Spn_vs_NB", "virusTRUE.bacteriaSpn")),
  HinvsNB_VT = list(c("bacteria_Hin_vs_NB", "virusTRUE.bacteriaHin"))
)
results_Bacteria_vsNB_VT <- imap(contrast_list_Bacteria_vsNB_VT, ~ run_contrast_analysis(dds, contrast_name = .y, contrast = .x))



Combine All Contrast Results

all_contrast_results <- list(
  results_Virus_TvsF,
  results_VirusInteract_vsNB,
  results_Species_vsNB_VF,
  results_Bacteria_vsNB_VT
  ) %>% flatten() 

all_contrast_df <- bind_rows(all_contrast_results)







IMPORTANT:



CONTENTO requires generic column names so it works with any DE tool, not just DESeq2. Required: log2FC, stat, padj. Optional: log2FC_shrunk. DESeq2’s results() already outputs stat and padj with the right names — only log2FoldChange (and log2FoldChange_shrunk) need renaming.



all_contrast_df <- all_contrast_df |>
  dplyr::rename(log2FC = log2FoldChange, log2FC_shrunk = log2FoldChange_shrunk)

title: Create SE for CONTENTO
text:
Step 5. Create Expression Matrix
As in Example 1, the expression matrix can be generated using any normalization or transformation method suitable for downstream visualization and exploratory analysis. Here we use the DESeq2 variance stabilizing transformation (VST).

expr_matrix <- assay(vst(dds, blind = FALSE))

title: Create SE for CONTENTO
text:
Step 6. Create SummarizedExperiment (SE) Object
We use the same convert_to_SE() function as in Example 1 to build the final SE object. In this case, we also include the variance partitioning results as additional columns in rowData, which can be visualized in CONTENTO’s Variance Decomposition tab.

SE = convert_to_SE(
  dds = dds,
  contrasts_df = all_contrast_df,
  expr_matrix = expr_matrix,
  varpart = varPart,
  organism = "Homo sapiens", 
  annotation = "Homo_sapiens.GRCh38.113_annot",
  dataset_name = "ExpMultContrast"
)

Loading variance partition data...

saveRDS(SE, file.path(SE_DIR, paste0(project_name, "_SE.rds")))
